kurz: Why growth alone is no reason to buy, where it comes from and how much of it the share price has already paid for.

bloecke.md:
The value of a company derives almost entirely from profits that will only arise in the future. For a utility with stable earnings, a good part of this falls within the next ten years; for a fast-growing software company, practically all of it falls in the period after that. Growth investing therefore means more than buying expensive shares. The buyer assumes that the company's profit will grow fast enough and for long enough to justify today's price.

Whether a company is growing can be read in every annual report. For the investment decision, the only thing that counts is how much growth the share price has already paid for. Growth and [[Value factor|value]] are therefore not opposing camps. Both rest on the same valuation calculation, in which growth is an input and does not constitute an investment style of its own.

## Where growth comes from

Revenue growth has five sources: higher sales volumes in the existing market, higher prices, new regions or customer groups, new products for existing customers, and acquisitions. In addition, there are two amplifiers of profit growth. Operating leverage takes effect when fixed costs are spread over more revenue and the margin rises. Share buybacks increase earnings per share even when total profit does not grow.

These sources differ in how durable they are. Price increases and operating leverage have a one-off effect and then run out. Acquisitions cost capital and often mask the fact that the organic business is stagnating. Only volume growth in a growing market where the company is able to defend its position can be extrapolated over years. Before a growth rate goes into a valuation model, you should therefore break down where the growth of the last three years came from.

bloecke.formel: g = reinvestment rate × return on capital (ROIC)
bloecke.erklaerung: Growth requires investment. It results from the share of profit that stays in the company, multiplied by the return earned on it. A company that reinvests 80% and earns 15% on it grows at 12%. A company that reinvests everything but earns only 7% grows at 7% and needs its entire profit to do so.
variablen: sustainable growth rate of operating profit
share of after-tax profit that flows into fixed assets, working capital and acquisitions
bloecke.beispiel: 0.80 × 15% = 12% p.a., compared with 1.00 × 7% = 7% p.a. with full reinvestment.

bloecke.md: Growth therefore only creates value if the return on capital is above the cost of capital. The KPMG cost of capital study (2025 edition, around 300 companies, of which over 230 are German) reports an average [[Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)|weighted average cost of capital (WACC)]] of 8.5% and a cost of equity of 9.7% for these companies. In the Technology segment, the WACC is 9.4%. A company that grows with a return on capital below these rates becomes larger and at the same time less valuable. Revenue growth alone is therefore not a mark of quality, because it initially consumes capital.

bloecke.titel: Growth and return on capital compared with the cost of capital
bloecke.unter: The same growth rate creates value on the left and destroys value on the right.

felder.text: High growth with ROIC above WACC. Every reinvested euro creates value. For this, the market demands a premium that can eat up the entire return.
High growth with ROIC below WACC. Revenue and total assets grow while the present value falls. Typical of capital-intensive expansion without pricing power.
Little growth, but ROIC above WACC. Low reinvestment needs, high distributable surplus. The value depends on how the capital is used.
Little growth, ROIC below WACC. Expansion would destroy the most value here. The right course would be shrinking, a sale or returning capital.

## Breaking down the investor's return

A shareholder's return is made up of three parts: earnings growth, the change in the valuation multiple, and the dividend. For growth shares, the dividend is usually missing altogether. Over long periods, the change in the multiple is reliably negative, because no company keeps a P/E of 60 when its growth inevitably flattens. This multiple compression is the normal case for growth shares.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula separates the contribution of the business from that of market sentiment. It applies without dividends. If there is a distribution, its yield is added approximately.
variablen: annual growth in earnings per share
valuation multiple at the start and at the end
bloecke.beispiel: g = 20%, P/E from 50 to 25, n = 10: 1.20 × 0.5^0.1 − 1 = 11.96% p.a. Profit increases sixfold, and just over half of the growth reaches the investor.

bloecke.titel: Annual return over ten years at an entry P/E of 50
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using (1 + g) × (P/E_end/50)^0.1 − 1. The rows show annual earnings growth, the columns the P/E at the end of the ten years.

bloecke.md: The table shows why excellent companies are so often mediocre investments. A company that increases its profit by 15% a year for ten years belongs roughly to the top tenth of large listed companies. If its share is bought at 50 times earnings and sold at 20 times, it returns 4.9% a year, which is less than a German federal bond yielded at times. Conversely, a low entry price does not make up for a shrinking business. Growth and valuation interact multiplicatively.

bloecke.titel: Valuation ratios of selected US industries (Damodaran, as of January 2026)

bloecke.md: The gap between the trailing and the forward P/E is the most telling. For semiconductors, the estimates assume that profit will almost triple within a year. The PEG ratio relates the P/E to expected earnings growth. Peter Lynch considered a value of around 1 to be fair. However, the ratio has a fundamental weakness. It depends entirely on estimated growth rates, takes account of neither risk nor capital requirements, and is useless at low or negative growth rates. It is suitable for initial screening, but not for a valuation.

## TAM calculations and their weaknesses

High valuations of growth shares are usually justified with the total addressable market, [[Total addressable market (TAM)|TAM]] for short. A typical example is a market of €100 billion in which the company wins a 10% share and earns a 20% margin on it. This can justify almost any price. The calculation looks harmless because each individual assumption is plausible. Since the assumptions are multiplied, however, every overestimate is multiplied too. Four moderately optimistic assumptions produce an unrealistically high result.

bloecke.titel: TAM calculation from market size to today's value
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. Each station rests on an assumption of its own, and only the last two steps lead to the value from today's perspective.

bloecke.titel: Weak points of the TAM calculation
bloecke.md:
- The seller defines the market. TAM figures usually come from company presentations and draw the boundaries of the market so that it looks large.
- The claimed market shares add up to more than 100%. If four competitors and the market leader each claim 25% to 30% for themselves, at most some of these claims can come true.
- The market is only large at prices that leave no margin. A market often grows precisely because prices are falling.
- The value only arises after many years and is reduced twice by then, through discounting and through dilution. Together, the two cost 69% in the example: 50 billion becomes 15.7 billion.

## Valuing loss-making companies

A loss does not rule out a share from the outset, but it requires three additional checks. First, you need to establish whether the loss is an investment or a permanent deficit. Spending on sales, marketing and development is recognised immediately in the income statement, even though it is meant to generate future revenue. The gross margin provides information, as does the question of whether the company would be profitable without spending on growth. If it makes losses even then, the business model itself is not viable.

Second, you need to check how long the money will last. Net cash divided by the annual cash outflow gives the runway. If the company needs new capital before reaching break-even, it has to raise it on the market. As a rule, existing shareholders are diluted most heavily precisely when the share price is at its lowest. The Altman Z-score sums up insolvency risk in a single number. An industrial company with a value below 1.81 is considered at risk.

Third, the valuation needs a yardstick. A price-to-sales ratio can only be interpreted with an assumed target margin. The following applies: fair P/S at maturity = net margin × fair P/E.

bloecke.titel: Worked example with a P/S of 20
bloecke.md:
Suppose the company achieves a net margin of 15% at maturity and then justifies a P/E of 20. That corresponds to a fair P/S of 0.15 × 20 = 3.0.

Today, the share trades at 20 times revenue. At a cost of capital of 9% over ten years, the following applies:

required revenue growth factor = 20 × 1.09^10 / 3.0 = 20 × 2.367 / 3.0 = 15.8

Revenue therefore has to increase almost sixteenfold in ten years, which corresponds to 31.8% growth a year. Even then, the buyer only earns a return equal to their cost of capital. With additional dilution, even higher growth would be needed. This backward calculation is more robust than any forecast because it does without a prediction. It shows what growth today's share price assumes, and this assumption can be checked.

## Philip Fisher's fifteen points

In 1958, Philip Fisher published *Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits*, adding qualitative criteria to Graham's numbers-based analysis. His catalogue comprises fifteen points on the product pipeline, research, sales, margin, labour relations, depth of management, accounting, capital requirements and, above all, the integrity of management. Fisher gathered the necessary information outside the office using the scuttlebutt method, that is, by systematically asking customers, suppliers, competitors and former employees. According to Fisher, you should almost never sell an excellent company. Buffett long described himself as 85% Graham and 15% Fisher. With the purchases of recent decades, this weighting has shifted considerably.

The following table groups eight of the fifteen areas thematically. Fisher's exact wording can be found in the book.

bloecke.titel: Fisher's areas of inquiry with features that can be checked today
zeilen: Whether the market is big enough for years of strong growth and whether something will follow today's product
Share of revenue from new products, research ratio, product announcements compared with deliveries
Whether development spending is in proportion to the revenue it has generated
R&D spending as a percentage of revenue compared with competitors, capitalised development costs
Whether the company can sell what it develops
Sales costs per new customer, customer retention, order backlog
Whether the margin is high and what keeps it high
Gross margin over five years, ability to push through price increases in inflationary periods
Whether the organisation can cope with the next growth spurt
Staff turnover, job advertisements, staffing of the second management level
Whether management knows how the company makes its money
Segment reports, operating cash flow compared with profit, changes of auditor or chief financial officer
Whether new equity is constantly needed for growth
Number of shares over time, capital increases, convertible bonds
Whether reporting is open, even when things are going badly
Comparison of old annual reports with later developments

bloecke.md: Today there are many easily accessible sources for this kind of research: review portals of former employees, job advertisements as an indication of where a company is investing, industry associations, trade fairs, prices on second-hand and spare-parts markets, and user reviews. The line is drawn by the EU Market Abuse Regulation (MAR). It is permissible to piece together many individual items of public information into an overall picture. Trading on the basis of a single item of non-public, price-sensitive information is not permissible. When calling a supplier, you may therefore ask about industry trends, but not about the customer's unpublished order figures.

## Lessons from 2000 and 2021

The Nasdaq Composite reached 5,048.62 points on 10 March 2000 and fell to around 1,114 points by 9 October 2002. That was a loss of 78%, and the index only regained its peak in 2015. In Germany, the losses were even greater. The Nemax 50, introduced in 1999 and backdated to the end of 1997 at 1,000 points, stood at 9,666 points on the same day in March 2000 and at 318 points 31 months later. The loss was over 96%, and around €200 billion of market value was wiped out. In addition, there were accounting scandals such as ComROAD, and in June 2003 the segment was closed.

The technology forecasts of 1999 largely came true, and 48% of the dotcom companies still existed in 2004, albeit at far lower valuations. With a Nasdaq P/E of around 200 at the end of 1999, a decade of growth had already been paid for in the share price. Returns arise from the difference between expectation and outcome. It is not enough for the expectations to come true.

bloecke.unter: The factor data in the last row measure value minus growth. A negative HML value means that growth shares were ahead in that year.

ereignisse.titel: Nasdaq back at its old peak
ereignisse.text: Only after around 15 years does the index trade at its March 2000 level again.
The value factor HML loses 30.7%, the worst year for value since the data began in 1926. Growth shares benefit particularly strongly from zero interest rates.
HML returns +31.7%, the S&P 500 falls by 25.4% and needs 24 months to get back to its old level. Higher discount rates reduce the value of distant cash flows the most.

bloecke.md: A simple formula explains the price fall of 2022. For a perpetual, steadily growing stream of payments, the multiple is 1 / (cost of capital − growth). At a 7% cost of capital and 2% growth, that is 20. If the cost of capital rises to 9%, the multiple falls to 14.3. That is a decline of 28.6%, even though nothing about the business has changed. The effect mainly concerns the part of the value that lies far in the future, and for a growth share that is almost the entire value. The price fall of these shares was therefore due to the higher discounting of future payments rather than to disappointment with the companies.

In growth investing, what matters is whether the growth expectations of the other market participants are too high or too low. The share of an excellent company is only a good investment if its price assumes less growth than actually materialises later.

Before every purchase of a growth share, write down the backward calculation. It records what revenue growth, what target margin and what multiple today's share price assumes. Only then research whether these assumptions are plausible. If you read the company's presentation first and only then do the calculation, you will always find a number that fits.

For German private investors, an individual share without a dividend triggers no tax until it is sold. The price gain remains invested in full and is only taxed at 26.375% (plus church tax) on sale. This deferral advantage is real, but small compared with an entry price that is 30% too high. It says nothing about the quality of the business model.

bloecke.titel: Thematic funds in a long-term comparison
bloecke.md:
Investors who bet on a growth theme instead of individual companies buy the same growth assumption bundled in a fund. They usually only buy once the prices of the theme have already risen sharply. A Morningstar study of thematic funds up to mid-2024 found that around 92% survive the first year and only just over half survive ten years. Over 15 years, 60% disappeared. Only about one fund in ten survived 15 years and at the same time beat the broad global equity market. Nevertheless, assets under management in thematic funds stood at $779 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

In Germany, there is an additional tax disadvantage. If a small thematic fund is liquidated, this counts as a sale. The tax deferral then ends compulsorily, at a time that the investor does not choose.

mitnehmen: For the investment decision, what counts is how much growth the share price has already paid for, because the fact that a company is growing is not enough of a reason to buy.
Growth arises from the reinvestment rate times the return on capital and only creates value if the return on capital is above the cost of capital (around 8.5% WACC on average in Germany).
The investor's return follows from earnings growth times the change in the multiple, which is why 15% earnings growth with a fall in the P/E from 50 to 20 only yields 4.9% a year.
TAM calculations multiply four optimistic assumptions, and discounting and dilution reduce the result in the example by just over two thirds.
In 2000, the technology forecast was right but the price was too high, so the Nasdaq needed 15 years to regain its old high, even though almost everything that had been promised came true.

begriffe.text: Total addressable market: the entire market that a product can address. It serves as an upper limit for revenue estimates and usually comes from company information. It is therefore not a neutral starting point for a valuation.

Decline in the valuation multiple (for example the P/E) during the holding period. It reduces the investor's return even when revenue and profit grow as planned, and it is the normal case for highly valued growth shares.

Research method coined by Philip Fisher in which customers, suppliers, competitors and former employees are questioned systematically. This produces a picture that does not emerge from the financial statements alone.

Increase in the number of shares through capital increases, convertible bonds or share-based compensation. It spreads future profit over more shares and lowers the value per share, even if the value of the company rises.
Market capitalisation divided by annual revenue. On its own, the ratio has no informative value. It can only be interpreted with an assumed target margin, because fair P/S = net margin × fair P/E.
